newCitations.caseName: Delshah 60 Ninth, LLC v. Free People of PA LLC
newCitations.outcome: Landlord Delshah won summary judgment in the district court on its breach-of-contract claim for $6,707,916.84 in unpaid rent against retail tenant Free People, which had stopped paying rent when NYC's COVID-19 emergency orders shut down non-essential retail in March 2020. The Second Circuit REVERSED, holding the lease's takings/casualty provision excused rent because the government orders prevented Free People from operating its brick-and-mortar clothing store -- even though the tenant retained some minimal physical access to the space -- distinguishing 'inability to operate the business' from 'total loss of access.' The court granted summary judgment to the tenant instead on its own breach-of-contract counterclaim.
newCitations.notes: A significant, CURRENT (2026) appellate-level tenant win directly contradicting the more landlord-friendly COVID-rent outcomes already in this dataset (e.g., SVAP III Poway Crossings). Confirms that lease-specific takings/casualty clause language -- not a generic force-majeure argument -- can still excuse rent for a pandemic-era closure period years after most COVID rent litigation resolved in landlords' favor; the outcome turns entirely on the particular clause's wording, which should be checked lease-by-lease. Also reported at law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca2/25-148/25-148-2026-05-05.html.

newCitations.caseName: Newark Shopping Ctr. Owner, L.L.C. v. Saudades Group, LLC
newCitations.outcome: After a one-day bench trial, the court found for the landlord on breach of a commercial lease and guaranty, holding the tenant (a restaurant operator) breached by never opening for business. However, the court held the lease's liquidated-damages provision was VOID as against public policy (an unenforceable penalty), and instead awarded the landlord only actual proven damages: $352,525.49 in unpaid rent plus $58,229.44 in attorney's fees and litigation costs.
newCitations.notes: Useful real-world illustration that a landlord can win on liability yet still lose the liquidated-damages multiplier it drafted for, recovering only actual unpaid rent instead -- reinforcing that this claim type's damages formula (unpaidRentAmount, not a multiplier) is the right default absent a separately-vetted enforceable liquidated-damages clause. Case caption sometimes rendered 'Newark Shopping Center Owner, LLC v. Saudades Group, LLC, et al.'; individual guarantors Phillip and Pamela Piraino were co-defendants.

newCitations.caseName: Kapneck 14-16, LLC v. Bkeezy's Speakeasy, LLC
newCitations.outcome: Landlord leased retail space to a beer-and-wine store tenant that stayed current on base rent but fell behind on other lease charges (utilities, taxes, late fees) defined as 'Additional Rent.' The landlord filed a summary ejectment action based partly on charges the tenant only learned of after suit was filed. The Supreme Court of Maryland held (1) the residential pre-suit notice statute does not apply to nonresidential tenancies, but (2) a landlord may obtain possession in a summary ejectment action only for rent that was actually due and unpaid under the lease AS OF THE FILING -- a summary ejectment action cannot be predicated on charges the tenant first learns of after the case is filed.
newCitations.notes: DOCTRINAL CITATION, not a dollar comparable -- no damages figure was confirmed from available sources. Included because it's a current, high-court-level clarification of what counts as 'rent due and unpaid' for commercial nonpayment proceedings specifically (as opposed to residential), and of the notice a landlord must give the tenant before including ancillary charges (taxes, utilities, fees) in that rent figure -- directly relevant to whether a given unpaidRentAmount figure will actually support the pursued remedy.

unpaid_rent.calibrationNote: The expanded sample still supports the current 0.90-0.97 base range for a facially valid, documented unpaid-rent claim -- Newark Shopping Center (landlord won on liability, just not on the liquidated-damages multiplier) and the original WEC 98C-3 and Grand Prospect citations all confirm landlords who can show actual unpaid rent recover it. But Delshah v. Free People (a 2026 appellate REVERSAL of a $6.7M landlord summary judgment based on specific lease takings-clause language) and Kapneck (rent must be actually due and properly noticed before it counts for recovery) both reinforce that the tenantDisputesDebt modifier (dropping probability to 0.55-0.75) is doing real, necessary work -- a facially large, well-documented claim can still collapse entirely on lease-specific wording or notice defects, not just on abatement-style factual disputes. No change to the numeric range is warranted, but the modifier conditions arguably deserve a third trigger for 'ambiguous force-majeure/takings clause language' given how much that one variable moved the Delshah outcome on appeal.

newCitations.caseName: Elk 33 E. 33rd LLC v. Sticky's Corporate LLC
newCitations.outcome: Trial court granted the landlord summary judgment for $576,069.05 on its accelerated-rent cause of action against the tenant and its corporate and 'good guy' guarantors. On appeal, the landlord conceded it had relet the premises and begun collecting a new tenant's rent as of January 2023 -- yet still sought to keep the full accelerated-rent judgment. The First Department held the lease permitted the landlord to accelerate rent OR to relet and collect actual/anticipated rent, but NOT both simultaneously without netting one against the other.
newCitations.notes: Directly reinforces this claim's reletOverride mechanic (net future rent = gross future rent minus actual/anticipated overlapping new rent, BEFORE PV discounting) with a current, real dollar figure -- a live, current-law illustration of the same double-dip problem the existing 2022 Cummings Properties v. Hines citation identifies. Related First Department authority on similar acceleration-clause limits: ALQ, LLC v. Kane, 197 A.D.3d 1029 (1st Dep't 2021) (no dual remedy); Chelsea 8th Ave. LLC v. Chelseamilk LLC, 220 A.D.3d 565 (1st Dep't 2023) (no acceleration while tenant remains in possession).

newCitations.caseName: Hourglass Entertainment, LLC v. NRG Investments, Inc.
newCitations.citation: 50 Fla. L. Weekly D1538, No. 2D2024-1251 (Fla. 2d DCA 2025)
newCitations.outcome: Landlord NRG sued tenant Hourglass over a parking-lot lease after Hourglass stopped paying rent in April 2021 while remaining contractually obligated through the lease's August 2024 expiration. The trial court's amended final judgment awarded $39,858 in damages, calculated using the full 40-month unpaid period through August 2024 -- but that period ran roughly four months PAST the date of the judgment itself. The Second District Court of Appeal held it was error to award rent for the four months between the judgment date and lease expiration because the lease contained NO express acceleration clause, and Florida law does not allow a landlord to recover future/unaccrued rent absent one.
newCitations.notes: A clean, current, small-dollar illustration of the gate condition already built into this claim's damages model ('No confirmed acceleration clause' drops probability to 0.15-0.3) -- confirms Florida courts will affirmatively strike out the unaccrued portion of a damages award, not just discount it, when no acceleration clause exists. Consistent with the existing Austin Hill Country Realty v. Palisades Plaza (Tex. 1997) mitigation-duty citation in spirit: both limit what a landlord can collect for the remaining term absent specific contractual authority.

newCitations.caseName: Newman Development Group of Pottstown, LLC v. Genuardi's Family Market, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: Landlord sued a supermarket tenant and its corporate successor for breach of a long-term ground/commercial lease. Following a bench trial in the Court of Common Pleas of Chester County, the case turned in part on how to calculate damages under the lease's Section 20.2.2 formula, including whether and how those damages should be reduced to present value -- a Pennsylvania Supreme Court justice specifically noted disagreement over 'the reduction to present value of the Section 20.2.2 damages.' The Supreme Court's principal holding addressed a procedural question (whether post-trial motions were required after a remand), sending the substantive damages dispute back for further proceedings culminating in the 2014 Superior Court decision.
newCitations.notes: INCOMPLETE VERIFICATION: the final dollar amount ultimately awarded was not independently confirmed from available sources -- only that present-value discounting of a contractual future-rent damages formula was a genuinely contested, appellately-significant issue in this case (parallel to the HealthSouth Rehabilitation Corp. v. Falcon Management Co. and Village at Brocks Gap present-value citations already in this dataset). Cited for that damages-methodology significance (62+ citing cases per CourtListener), not as a clean dollar comparable -- verify the final Superior Court damages figure directly before relying on any number from this matter.

accelerated_rent.calibrationNote: The 0.65-0.90 base range and the gate dropping probability to 0.15-0.3 without a confirmed acceleration clause both hold up well against the expanded sample: Hourglass Entertainment shows a court affirmatively stripping out unaccrued rent for lack of a clause, while Elk 33 shows even a landlord WITH a valid acceleration clause losing part of its recovery for failing to net out actual re-let income (a distinct, second failure mode already captured by this claim's reletOverride mechanic). Newman Development confirms present-value discounting of the net figure is a genuinely litigated, high-stakes issue nationally, not just an Alabama or Ohio quirk -- supporting the current 5-9% discount rate range as the right level of parameterization rather than a flat haircut.

newCitations.caseName: NCO Financial Systems, Inc. v. Montgomery Park, LLC
newCitations.outcome: In a long-running dispute over a 12-year commercial office lease in Baltimore (this being the second of several appeals in the same litigation), the Fourth Circuit clarified the scope of a commercial landlord's obligation to mitigate damages after a tenant's early termination/breach: if a landlord fails to properly mitigate (e.g., by making reasonable efforts to re-let, which can include efforts that generate re-leasing costs), that failure only REDUCES the damages recoverable -- it does not categorically bar the landlord's damages claim altogether.
newCitations.notes: DOCTRINAL CITATION -- no dollar amount for re-leasing costs specifically was confirmed from available sources, and this litigation has multiple related opinions (842 F.3d 816 (4th Cir. 2016); a further 2025 appeal at 134 F.4th 265) addressing different sub-issues in the same underlying lease dispute; verify which opinion covers which issue before citing a specific holding. Useful for this claim type because it establishes the CEILING on the mitigation-failure risk: a landlord's re-leasing costs and effort are not all-or-nothing -- imperfect mitigation shrinks the recovery rather than zeroing it out, which supports this claim's damages formula using a modest haircut (0.85-1.0 of costs) rather than a steeper discount tied to mitigation-effort disputes.

newCitations.caseName: Naiman Richmond Properties, Ltd. v. Brand Castle, L.L.C.
newCitations.citation: 2024-Ohio-2910 (8th Dist. Ct. App., Cuyahoga Cnty., Aug. 15, 2024)
newCitations.outcome: A prospective commercial tenant (Brand Castle) never took possession of leased space -- the landlord never provided keys and the tenant never occupied the premises -- and the parties' lease-related damages provision was triggered on that non-commencement/breach. The trial court awarded the landlord approximately $265,595.86, reported as the cost of renovations/improvements the landlord had performed as consideration for arranging a more lucrative replacement lease with a new tenant, rejecting the defaulting tenant's argument that the landlord failed to satisfy its duty to mitigate. The Eighth District affirmed.
newCitations.notes: PARTIAL VERIFICATION: the primary source (the opinion itself) confirms the breach, the mitigation-defense rejection, and that the lease's own damages formula governed -- but the precise $265,595.86 figure and its exact characterization as 'renovation cost' damages come from secondary reporting/search-derived summaries, not from a direct read of the full opinion text, so treat that specific number with more caution than the primary-source-confirmed citations in this dataset. If accurate, it is a good illustration that 'releasing/mitigation cost' damages can be measured by what the landlord spent to LAND a replacement deal, not only by out-of-pocket repair costs for the vacated space.

releasing_mitigation_costs.calibrationNote: This claim type remains genuinely thin on close, dollar-confirmed comparables even after this round of research (only 4 real citations total across old and new, versus 6+ for several other claim types) -- both new additions here are meaningfully caveated (one has no dollar figure, the other's dollar figure is only secondary-source-confirmed). Given that, the current 0.6-0.85 base probability range is not contradicted by anything found, but it is also not strongly validated the way unpaid_rent or accelerated_rent now are; the 0.85-1.0-of-costs damages multiplier (i.e., landlords recover close to what they actually spent) is consistent with both Village at Brocks Gap and the Naiman Richmond figure, so no change is recommended, but this claim type would benefit from further, better-verified research before being treated as fully calibrated.

newCitations.caseName: Cheetah Properties 1, LLC v. Panther Pressure Testers, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: Landlord Cheetah Properties appealed a district court judgment finding that commercial tenant Panther Pressure Testers did NOT 'willfully' hold over after its lease ended, which defeated the landlord's claim for statutory double damages for the holdover period. The district court also denied the landlord's request for attorney's fees. The North Dakota Supreme Court affirmed, rejecting the landlord's holdover claim.
newCitations.notes: DOLLAR AMOUNT NOT CONFIRMED. A landlord-LOSES counter-example on the 'willfulness' element some states require before a holdover multiplier applies -- joins Spatz v. 2263 North Lincoln Corp. (good-faith colorable claim of right) and Lincoln Oldsmobile v. Branch (no retroactive demand) already in this dataset as a third, independent way a holdover multiplier claim can fail even where the tenant did, in fact, remain in possession past term. Cited 12 times per CourtListener, suggesting real doctrinal weight in jurisdictions with a willfulness requirement.

newCitations.caseName: Mel-Lo Enterprises, Inc. v. Belle Starr Saloon, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: Commercial landlord sued a saloon tenant seeking $34,200 in unpaid rent, interest, property-damage costs, AND double rent for a holdover period under the lease's holdover clause. The trial court awarded the landlord only $11,400 in unpaid rent and denied all other requested categories, including the double-rent holdover claim; the Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed this partial, reduced recovery.
newCitations.notes: PARTIAL VERIFICATION -- confirmed via case-law search summary rather than a full read of the opinion; treat the precise reasoning for denying the double-rent claim with some caution pending direct verification. A good, older but clean illustration that a facially plausible holdover multiplier claim (properly pled, tied to an actual lease clause) can still be denied in whole by the trial court, with the landlord recovering only a fraction (about 33%) of what it originally sought across all categories combined.

holdover_damages.calibrationNote: Both new citations are landlord-LOSES outcomes on the holdover multiplier specifically, which -- stacked on top of the existing Baca v. Kuang, Lincoln Oldsmobile v. Branch, and Spatz v. 2263 North Lincoln Corp. citations (also landlord-loses on the multiplier) -- means five of the seven total holdover_damages citations in this dataset now involve a denied or reduced holdover-multiplier claim, against only Victoria's Secret and ESRT 501 Seventh Ave. as clean multiplier wins. That pattern is a mild caution flag on the current 0.8-0.95 baseProbability range: it may be somewhat calibrated to 'does a holdover fact pattern generally support SOME recovery' (which the sample supports, since landlords still won actual/unpaid rent almost every time) rather than 'does the enhanced statutory/contractual MULTIPLIER specifically apply' (which the sample suggests fails more often than 80-95% of the time, especially where willfulness, timely demand, or a colorable right-to-possess defense is in play). Consider whether this claim type should model the multiplier's applicability as a separate, lower-probability sub-question from the underlying holdover-occupancy fact itself.

newCitations.caseName: Pryority Partnership v. AMT Properties, LLC
newCitations.outcome: Commercial tenant sued its landlord for breach of lease, negligent misrepresentation (about the condition of and the landlord's intent to repair the building's roof), and constructive eviction after the landlord failed to timely repair the building and keep it tenantable. The trial court found for the tenant on all theories, awarding $193,006.35 in compensatory damages plus $69,002.68 in attorney's fees under the lease's fee-shifting clause; the Court of Appeals affirmed in full, finding no reversible error.
newCitations.notes: Also directly useful for the quiet_enjoyment_breach claim type (see that citation set) -- the fee award here (~36% of the compensatory damages) is a real contested-litigation data point on the higher end, usefully bracketing against the Village at Brocks Gap uncontested ~1.3% ratio already in this dataset and illustrating this claim's SUPERSEDING posture-tiered flat-dollar model (a real trial/appeal here plausibly falls in the $50,000-$200,000 trial tier, and $69,002.68 sits comfortably within it).

newCitations.caseName: Simbo Properties, Inc. v. M8 Realty, L.L.C.
newCitations.citation: 2019-Ohio-3091 (8th Dist. Ct. App., Cuyahoga Cnty., Aug. 1, 2019)
newCitations.outcome: In a commercial lease dispute where the landlord's own property-damage claim failed at directed verdict for lack of causation evidence, the tenant was nonetheless found to be the 'prevailing party' under the lease's fee-shifting clause on the 'main issue' of the case, even though the landlord had won on some minor sub-issues (a flagpole item and real estate tax charges). The Eighth District affirmed the tenant's entitlement to reasonable attorney's fees and expenses, applying a 'main issue' prevailing-party test for sophisticated, counseled commercial parties and holding the tenant did not need to prove it had already paid its attorneys before judgment.
newCitations.notes: DOLLAR AMOUNT NOT CONFIRMED for the fee award itself. Valuable for the 'main issue' prevailing-party doctrine it applies -- directly comparable to, and reinforcing, the existing Wells & McElwee v. Tiffany & Tomato (Ga. 2021) citation's point that prevailing-party status turns on overall/main-issue success, not any single sub-issue. Also independently useful for the property_damage claim type (see that citation set) since the landlord's own property-damage claim is what failed here for lack of proof.

attorney_fees.calibrationNote: The existing feeTiers model (default $5-10K; answered-passive $15-25K; contested-msj $20-45K; trial $50-200K) is well supported by the new sample: Pryority Partnership's $69,002.68 fee award after a full trial and appeal sits squarely in the trial tier, and it arose from real, actively-litigated liability findings (breach, negligent misrepresentation, constructive eviction) rather than a default -- exactly the kind of matter this tier is meant to capture. Nothing in this round's research suggests the tiers need adjustment; if anything, Pryority Partnership is a useful anchor for the trial tier's lower-middle range to add alongside the existing Rohrmoos Venture and Village at Brocks Gap data points.

newCitations.caseName: Simbo Properties, Inc. v. M8 Realty, L.L.C.
newCitations.citation: 2019-Ohio-3091 (8th Dist. Ct. App., Cuyahoga Cnty., Aug. 1, 2019)
newCitations.outcome: Commercial landlord sought damages from its former tenant for alleged property damage (among other claims, including a flagpole item and real estate taxes). The trial court granted a DIRECTED VERDICT against the landlord on the property-damage claim specifically, holding the landlord failed to introduce evidence establishing the tenant CAUSED the alleged damage. The Eighth District affirmed.
newCitations.notes: A landlord-LOSES counter-example -- useful balance against the large Apple Glen Investors v. Express Scripts ($6.2M) win already in this dataset. Confirms that even a facially plausible property-damage claim can fail entirely for a basic evidentiary gap (failure to prove CAUSATION, not just failure to prove amount), which is a distinct failure mode from the normalWearHaircut this claim's damages formula already models.

newCitations.caseName: Avalon Pacific-Santa Ana, L.P. v. HD Supply Repair & Remodel, LLC
newCitations.citation: 192 Cal. App. 4th 1183, 122 Cal. Rptr. 3d 417 (Cal. Ct. App., 4th Dist. 2011)
newCitations.outcome: Landlord leased vacant warehouse/office space to a tenant that intended to convert it into a retail facility; the tenant demolished the existing office structures as part of that conversion, then ceased operations before completing the project. A dispute followed over the resulting condition of the property and the parties' respective obligations.
newCitations.notes: INCOMPLETE VERIFICATION: only the general fact pattern (tenant demolition mid-renovation, then cessation of operations) was confirmed from available sources -- the court's actual holding, any damages figure, and which party ultimately prevailed on the property-condition dispute were NOT confirmed. Cited cautiously and only for the fact pattern (a tenant leaving a property mid-demolition/renovation is a distinct property-damage scenario from ordinary wear-and-tear or willful destruction); do not rely on this entry for outcome or dollar-amount guidance without pulling the full opinion first.

property_damage.calibrationNote: The one new well-confirmed data point (Simbo Properties) is a landlord LOSS on causation grounds, which -- alongside the existing 45 Broadway Owner v. NYSA-ILA citation (landlord loss on a waiver-of-subrogation clause) -- means two of the four citations now in this claim type's full sample are landlord losses for reasons entirely outside the normalWearHaircut variable this claim's damages formula models (failure of proof, and a lease clause barring the claim regardless of fault). That is a reasonable basis to treat the current 0.7-0.9 baseProbability range as possibly a touch optimistic for property damage claims specifically, versus lease claims generally, though the sample is still too small (and this round's research too thin, with real budget constraints) to recommend a specific numeric change with confidence -- flagging this as a claim type that would benefit from further research before the range is treated as well-calibrated.

wrongful_lockout.calibrationNote: No new citations were added in this round -- research time was prioritized toward the thinner claim types (releasing_mitigation_costs, holdover_damages, attorney_fees, property_damage, security_deposit, tortious_interference_lost_profits), since wrongful_lockout already has the strongest, most jurisdictionally diverse existing sample in this entire claim-type set (five real citations spanning FL, MN, TX, AZ, and MD, including both a $8.8M plaintiff win and a full landlord-win reversal in Donegal Associates). Nothing found in adjacent research (e.g., while researching tortious_interference_lost_profits) contradicted the existing baseProbabilityByState structure or the per-state remedy-mechanism modeling; the existing sample continues to support treating 'Not Available' self-help jurisdictions as high-probability-of-liability (0.85-0.95) and 'Available_ProcessFollowed' as low (0.1-0.25), consistent with Donegal Associates (landlord followed a lawful peaceable-and-entitled process and won) versus Palm Beach Florida Hotel and Berg v. Wiley (self-help unavailable, landlords lost big). This claim type's calibration looks sound as-is; recommend prioritizing it lower in any future research pass, in favor of wrongful_lockout's own weaker sibling claim, tortious_interference_lost_profits.

newCitations.caseName: K & K Management, Inc. v. Chul Woo Lee
newCitations.outcome: Motel owners (K & K Management) had contracted with the Lees to operate the motel's restaurant under a profit-sharing lease arrangement. About two years in, the motel owners decided terminating the arrangement was more efficient than continuing it, and LOCKED OUT the restaurant operators without notice as their chosen termination method -- disrupting the restaurant operators' ongoing business operations and their relationships with the business's own customers, suppliers, and staff. The Maryland Court of Appeals (the state's highest court at the time) addressed the propriety of self-help lockout as a termination strategy and the tort theories available to a locked-out commercial tenant whose business relationships are disrupted by the lockout itself, not merely its exclusion from the premises.
newCitations.notes: IMPORTANT VERIFICATION GAP: this session confirmed the case is real (citation, court, date, and core facts verified via CourtListener, which also shows it has been cited 145 times -- indicating real, lasting doctrinal significance), but could NOT independently confirm the specific dollar damages ultimately awarded (this is a well-known case in property-law teaching materials for its intentional-infliction-of-emotional-distress and business-tort holdings arising from a commercial lockout, but that general reputation was not re-verified against the primary opinion text in this session -- pull the full opinion before citing a specific damages figure or holding to a client). Still, this is by far the most squarely on-point real case found for this claim type's specific theory (a lockout disrupting the tenant's OWN business relationships, not just its occupancy) -- meaningfully better than the existing EXRP 14 Holdings citation, which the file's own note already flags as off-point (a construction-delay case, not a lockout case).

tortious_interference_lost_profits.calibrationNote: K & K Management is a real, heavily-cited (145x) case squarely on the fact pattern this claim type is built around -- a landlord using lockout as a business-termination tool, disrupting the tenant's own operations and relationships -- which is meaningfully better authority than the file's prior EXRP 14 Holdings citation (already flagged as off-point). That said, even with this addition, the fact that a genuinely on-point, frequently-cited case is nearly 40 years old and still the best available authority found reinforces the existing note's core conclusion: this is a real but INFREQUENTLY STANDALONE-LITIGATED theory, and this session's research did not surface a single MODERN (post-2015) case squarely combining a commercial self-help lockout with a separate, quantified lost-profits recovery specifically for third-party contract disruption. The current 0.25-0.55 baseProbability range remains reasonable as an estimate of viability once pled, but should still be treated as more speculative/less-calibrated than this dataset's other lease-dispute claim types, exactly as the existing note already cautions.

newCitations.caseName: Pryority Partnership v. AMT Properties, LLC
newCitations.outcome: Commercial tenant sued its landlord for breach of lease, negligent misrepresentation, and constructive eviction after the landlord misrepresented the condition of the building's roof and its intent to repair it, then failed to timely repair the roof and keep the building tenantable. The trial court found constructive eviction and awarded the tenant $193,006.35 in compensatory damages plus $69,002.68 in attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals affirmed in full.
newCitations.notes: A strong, real, dollar-substantial (nearly $193K) constructive-eviction/failure-to-repair win for a tenant, arising from a genuinely commercial fact pattern (a roof-repair failure and related misrepresentation about repair intentions) -- meaningfully larger than the existing Wesson v. Leone ($1,063) and Radinsky v. Weaver ($2,212) citations, which the file itself already flags as illustrating modest actual recoveries relative to what's claimed. Also independently useful for the attorney_fees claim type (see that citation set).

newCitations.caseName: Karaoke Heroes NH, LLC v. RVRM Enterprises, LLC
newCitations.citation: Docket No. AC48149 (Conn. App. Ct. Mar. 3, 2026)
newCitations.outcome: Commercial tenant operating a karaoke establishment sued its landlord after a third party removed bollards protecting the tenant's required emergency-exit egress path and then told fire authorities the tenant no longer had egress rights through that exit -- threatening the tenant's continued lawful operation. The tenant argued the landlord breached the lease and Connecticut's unfair trade practices act by failing to secure a written egress agreement. The Connecticut Appellate Court affirmed judgment for the LANDLORD, holding an implied emergency-access agreement existed (evidenced by the tenant's continued fee payments to the third party accepted without objection), that the lease itself only obligated the landlord to secure alleyway ingress/egress, and that the tenant bore responsibility for its own post-signature legal/regulatory compliance.
newCitations.notes: A current (2026), real, landlord-WINS counter-example on a repair/interference-adjacent theory -- useful balance against this claim type's other citations, most of which are tenant wins or doctrine-establishing cases. Illustrates a real limiting principle: quiet-enjoyment/repair-failure liability requires the INTERFERENCE TO STEM FROM AN ACTUAL LEASE OBLIGATION the landlord failed to meet, not from a third party's separate, subsequent conduct or from a regulatory compliance burden the lease placed on the tenant itself -- directly parallel to the existing Barash v. Pennsylvania Terminal Real Estate Corp. principle already in this dataset. No dollar amount at issue since the tenant recovered nothing.

quiet_enjoyment_breach.calibrationNote: The two new citations pull in opposite directions in a way that validates rather than undermines the current 0.4-0.65 baseProbability range: Pryority Partnership is a real, fully-litigated, appellately-affirmed tenant win with a substantial six-figure recovery for a straightforward failure-to-repair/constructive-eviction fact pattern, while Karaoke Heroes is an equally real, current landlord win where the alleged interference didn't trace back to an actual lease obligation. Together with the existing sample (2 tenant wins, 1 landlord win, 1 uncertain-dollar settlement), the fuller picture now shows roughly even odds skewed slightly toward tenant recovery when there's a genuine repair/interference failure by the landlord -- squarely consistent with the current range and requiring no change; if anything, the addition of a confirmed ~$193K recovery supports the note that damages, while sometimes modest (Wesson, Radinsky), can also be substantial when the interference caused real relocation/business harm.

newCitations.caseName: FP Stores, Inc. v. Tramontina US, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: Commercial landlord FP Stores retained tenant Tramontina's security deposit after the lease ended. Tramontina sued for breach of contract and for violation of Texas Property Code § 93.011 (the commercial security-deposit bad-faith-retention statute), alleging the deposit was withheld in bad faith. The trial court granted Tramontina summary judgment. The Court of Appeals AFFIRMED, holding the landlord failed to present sufficient evidence justifying its retention of the deposit.
newCitations.notes: DOLLAR AMOUNT NOT CONFIRMED (the underlying deposit/judgment figure was not available from sources reviewed in this session). Directly on point for the existing note in this claim type flagging that a bad-faith-withholding doubling penalty should be checked per-state -- Texas Property Code § 93.011 is exactly that kind of statute for COMMERCIAL tenancies specifically (distinct from the residential deposit statutes most states have), and this is a real, appellate-affirmed application of it against a landlord who could not substantiate its retention decision with evidence.

security_deposit.calibrationNote: This claim type's research yielded only one new, real, commercial-specific citation this round despite substantial search effort -- multiple other candidates surfaced during research (a Maryland Bkeezy's-type additional-rent dispute, a New York judgment-increase case, a Texas residential deposit case) but had to be excluded either because their commercial character couldn't be confirmed or their specific facts/holding couldn't be verified from available sources, consistent with this task's instruction not to include unverifiable citations. The one addition (FP Stores v. Tramontina, a landlord loss for failure to substantiate withholding) is consistent with the existing sample's pattern (three of four existing citations already involve a landlord's improper or unauthorized withholding), reinforcing rather than changing the calibration picture: the current 0.55-0.8 baseProbability range, with a further +0.1-0.15 boost when the landlord provided no itemization, looks directionally right -- landlords who withhold a commercial deposit without solid contractual authorization and proof appear to lose more often than they win across this now-five-case sample. This claim type would benefit from additional, better-resourced research (ideally with full-text case access) before being treated as fully calibrated, given the thinner-than-ideal yield this round.
